Joseph Grigg
JOH-sef grig
proper noun
Surname Grigg, a diminutive form of Gregory (Greek Grēgorios, “watchful”); Joseph from Hebrew, “he shall add.”

📖 Biblical Definition

Joseph Grigg (c. 1720–1768) rose from a mechanic’s trade to the Presbyterian ministry, serving as assistant at Silver Street Chapel in London before an early retirement to writing and quiet devotion. Yet the LORD had ordained that a hymn composed, by tradition, when Grigg was but a boy of ten should outlive every sermon he preached. “Jesus, and shall it ever be, a mortal man ashamed of Thee?” is the cry of a soul that reckons the fear of man a shameful thing and the confession of Christ the highest honour a creature can bear. In an age that prizes reputation above obedience, Grigg’s hymn presses upon the conscience that unbelief blushes at its Saviour while faith glories in Him. The verse rises to holy resolve—“Ashamed of Jesus! that dear Friend on whom my hopes of heaven depend”—and closes in the assurance that He who is not ashamed to call His people brethren will one day own them before the Father and the holy angels. Grigg wrote also “Behold a Stranger at the door,” a tender pleading with the Christless heart. His life reminds the church that a single Spirit-borne stanza, faithfully framed, may do more for Christ than a lifetime of applause, and that boldness in confession is the badge of every true disciple.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

English hymnwriter (c. 1720–1768), author of “Jesus, and Shall It Ever Be,” a hymn against shame in confessing Christ.

expand to see more

An English minister who rose from a mechanic’s trade to Presbyterian ministry in London.

Assistant at Silver Street Chapel before retiring to writing and devotion.

Author of “Jesus, and Shall It Ever Be,” a hymn resolving never to be ashamed of Christ.

Also wrote “Behold a Stranger at the Door,” pleading with the unconverted.

A witness that bold confession, not the fear of man, marks the true disciple.

📖 Key Scripture

Mar 8:38 — "Whosoever therefore shall be ashamed of me and of my words in this adulterous and sinful generation; of him also shall the Son of man be ashamed, when he cometh in the glory of his Father with the holy angels."

2Ti 1:12 — "For the which cause I also suffer these things: nevertheless I am not ashamed: for I know whom I have believed, and am persuaded that he is able to keep that which I have committed unto him against that day."

Rom 1:16 — "For I am not ashamed of the gospel of Christ: for it is the power of God unto salvation to every one that believeth; to the Jew first, and also to the Greek."

Heb 2:11 — "For both he that sanctifieth and they who are sanctified are all of one: for which cause he is not ashamed to call them brethren,"

⚠️ Modern Corruption

A faithful witness, not a contested doctrine; his hymn recovers the principle of unashamed confession of Christ.

expand to see more

Grigg is preserved because his single great hymn names the sin the age most flatters: the shame that blushes to own the Lord Jesus before a scoffing world. Where the church trims her confession to purchase the world’s good opinion, Grigg’s stanza indicts her, for to be ashamed of Christ is already to be counted with the adulterous generation.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is bold, open confession—that the disciple who is not ashamed of Christ shall find that Christ is not ashamed of him. In a day of quiet, apologetic Christianity, Grigg summons the believer to reckon the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasures of men, and to fear the shame of that great day more than the frowns of this present one.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Grigg’s hymn roots Christian courage in Christ’s own promise to confess those who confess Him.

expand to see more

The warning that Christ will be ashamed of those ashamed of Him (Mar 8:38).

Paul’s settled confidence, “I am not ashamed: for I know whom I have believed” (2Ti 1:12).

The gospel as no cause of shame but the power of God unto salvation (Rom 1:16).

Christ’s condescension in not being ashamed to call the saints brethren (Heb 2:11).

The reckoning that the fear of man is a snare to be renounced in worship and witness.
